rounds.proof_sketch: Grid is launched with dim3(batch_size) = dim3(128), so blockIdx.x ∈ [0, 127]. Original guard: batch_idx >= 128 is FALSE for all valid batch_idx. Mutated guard: batch_idx > 128 is also FALSE for all valid batch_idx. Both conditions never trigger because batch_idx can never reach batch_size (128) — the maximum is batch_size-1 (127).
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the early-return guard from `batch_idx >= batch_size` to `batch_idx > batch_size`. For the fixed input shape with batch_size=128, the kernel is launched with exactly 128 blocks (grid_dims = batch_size). This means blockIdx.x ranges from 0 to 127 inclusive. The original condition `batch_idx >= 128` is never true since max batch_idx is 127. Similarly, the mutated condition `batch_idx > 128` is never true. Both versions execute all 128 blocks identically. The distinguishing case (batch_idx == 128) is architecturally impossible because CUDA block indices are always less than the grid dimension.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation would only be distinguishable if batch_idx could equal batch_size, which requires launching more blocks than batch_size — impossible since grid_dims is set to exactly batch_size. No value-level input can affect CUDA block scheduling.
rounds.recommendations: Boundary guard mutations like `>=` to `>` are often equivalent when the guard protects against out-of-bounds block indices and the grid is sized exactly to the data. To detect such mutations, mutation testing frameworks should consider that kernel launch parameters (grid/block dims) define hard architectural limits that cannot be bypassed by value-level testing. Consider flagging `idx >= N` guards as potentially equivalent when grid_dims equals N, since blockIdx will never reach N.
